Logo refresh · Round 1 concepts

Onshore Air

Three logo concepts for the Sunshine Coast's air-conditioning specialists. Each keeps the sun-meets-sea idea Luke already owns, rebuilt as a modern brand system that holds up on a 6 m van and at 16 px in a browser tab.

Client Onshore Air, Pacific Paradise QLDPrepared by LeadHive AUDate 26 October 2026
Strategy

Hot outside, cool inside. Told once, simply.

Blue owns Australian air conditioning: 13 of the 15 brands we audited lead with blue. Red is the OEM accent, and local installers default to snowflakes, swooshes and stock Montserrat. Nobody owns the coastal warm-to-cool story, and Onshore Air's sun-meets-sea sphere already tells it.

The job is to keep that idea and make it professional: flat geometry, a confident wordmark and a complete file set.

  1. Keep the circular sun/sea symbol and its warm/cool split. It is Onshore's equity, and it literally describes the product.
  2. Rebuild it as flat geometry: 3–5 solid shapes, no gradients, no hairlines, embroidery-safe gaps.
  3. Lead with deep navy. Make sun-gold the signature and ocean blue the cool counterpoint. No red, no lemon yellow.
  4. Replace the outlined surf-shop type with a heavy, kerned geometric sans, delivered as outlines.
  5. Ship a full system (stacked, horizontal, compact, icon, favicon, mono, reversed) built to sit beside Daikin, Mitsubishi Electric and Airstage badges.

What we keep

  • The circle: sun, sea and air in one shape
  • The warm-versus-cool split
  • Navy, yellow/gold and ocean blue

What we fix

  • Outlined, low-legibility lettering
  • Gradient stripes that cannot embroider or print in one colour
  • No small-size, horizontal, mono or reversed versions, and no clear-space rules
Before and after

Same idea, three ways forward

The current logo (left), as supplied, beside the three concepts, each on its own navy as it would appear in the website header. Concept 1 keeps today's diagonal sun-meets-sea split most directly, which is why it is our recommendation.

Recommended
01
Concept 1

Evolution

This is the sun-meets-sea sphere Onshore Air already owns, rebuilt as four flat bands so it prints, embroiders and still reads as a favicon.

The diagonal S-split tells the product story at a glance: Sunshine Coast heat in the bottom-left, cool ocean air in the top-right.

Paired with a heavy, round-shouldered Outfit wordmark, it looks like the same company, grown up.

Small-size tests
02
Concept 2

Horizon

The sun sits on a single line that is both the coastline horizon and the onshore breeze. It runs flat under the sun, then sweeps up the right side and tapers away like a gust of sea air.

Inside the sun, the warm/cool split is kept as sun over sea, and the whole mark uses only two main colours plus an ocean-blue accent.

Set in a wide-tracked Sora wordmark, it has the calm restraint of an OEM dealer badge and is the most premium of the three in large formats.

03
Concept 3

Monogram

A navy O, the initial of Onshore, frames the original diagonal sun-meets-sea split: warm bottom-left, cool top-right.

It is the simplest, sturdiest silhouette of the three, so it holds up at 16 px, on a cap and as a Google avatar.

The Red Hat Display Black wordmark adds corporate weight. The trade-off is that the ring makes it read more like a badge than a personality.

System rules

Clear space and minimum sizes

Clear space on every side is x, the cap height of ONSHORE in the wordmark. Nothing else (text, photos, the edge of a van panel) goes inside the dashed line. The supplied files already include a half-x margin.

Recommendation

Go with Concept 1, Evolution

  1. It keeps the identity Onshore already has. Customers already know the diagonal sun-meets-sea split from the van, the shirts and the Google listing. Evolution is the only concept that keeps it as the whole mark, so the refresh reads as an upgrade, not a rebrand.
  2. It has the most personality. Four flat colours carry on a van at distance and stand out in a social feed or a Maps list, where most trades are blue on white.
  3. It passes the practical tests. The favicon cut reads at 16 px and the embroidery cut has widened gaps. Every lockup has one-colour and on-navy versions.
  4. Its trade-offs are manageable. It is the most colourful of the three, so one-colour jobs use the mono files, and at the very smallest sizes the bands read by colour rather than by shape.

Runner-up: Concept 3, Monogram, for a client who wants maximum simplicity. It is technically the safest at small sizes, and its O now carries the diagonal split. But the ring dominates, and the overall silhouette reads as generic, a porthole or a bank badge that could belong to any company. Its small-size advantage is real, but Evolution already passes the 16 px test with its favicon cut.

Concept 2, Horizon is the premium outlier: the most refined at large sizes, but the least connected to the logo customers know today.

Next steps

What we need from Luke

  1. Confirm the direction. We recommend Evolution, and elements can be mixed, for example Monogram's heavier wordmark with the Evolution mark.
  2. One round of refinements on the chosen concept (colour, weight, descriptor wording).
  3. Final artwork pack: SVG master files plus print PDFs with CMYK values proofed by the printer, an embroidery file digitised from the mono artwork, and the van wrap scaled from SVG.
